text:
I felt the air leave my lungs like someone had punched me in the stomach. I gripped the edge of the desk so hard my knuckles went white.

— Tver. I said Tver. Are you even listening?

I looked at him, and for a second, I actually felt it—that hot, prickly heat climbing up my neck. The violin. That stupid, cursed instrument. I could almost feel the bow in my hand, the way the strings vibrated against my chin, the way my mother used to stand in the doorway with that *look* on her face. The look that said I wasn't good enough.

— Marinka needs to keep her mouth shut. And I'm not playing anything at any party.

I shoved my headphones over my ears and turned back to the window, the rain blurring the gray world outside.

— Don't ask me about it again.

I felt my stomach tighten into a knot. My hand instinctively went to the penguin keychain on my backpack, squeezing it until the plastic felt like it would snap.

— I said Tver. Not St. Petersburg. Are you even listening?

I turned my body fully away from him, pulling my hoodie tighter around my shoulders. The classroom felt smaller suddenly, the air thick with the smell of wet chalk and floor wax.

— And Marinka should keep her mouth shut. I don't play anymore. There's no "playing" at a party, so just... forget it. Forget the whole thing.

I shoved my earbuds back in and pressed play on my phone, the music drowning out everything else.

I turned back to the window, the glass fogging up from the warmth inside. My chest felt tight, like someone was squeezing it. The violin was in its case under my bed at home, gathering dust, and the thought of bringing it here—to *this* place—made my stomach turn.

— I didn't quit. I'm just not playing. There's a difference. And no, I'm not playing at any party. Find someone else to be your entertainment.

I let out a soft, surprised laugh, shaking my head. My fingers traced the rim of the empty cup as I looked at you, really *looked* at you, with a slow, appreciative tilt of my head.

— A man with vinyl and a plan. That's dangerous. — I pulled the keys from the hook behind the counter and jingled them. — I don't sleep here, but I do spend enough time in this place that I'm starting to smell like espresso beans. 

I stepped around the counter, grabbing my jacket and tossing it over my arm. I paused at the door, glancing back at the empty cafe, then back at you with a small, knowing smile.

— Give me ten minutes to lock up and get Pumpkin. If you're lucky, the cat won't scratch your records. — I pushed the door open, letting the damp air hit us. — Lead the way, neighbor.

I let out a short, breathy laugh, shaking my head as I tucked a strand of red hair behind my ear. 

— Straight to the point. I like that. — I looked at the empty cafe, then back at you, my green eyes narrowing slightly. — But I'm not that kind of girl, and you're not that kind of guy. Not yet, anyway.

I stepped around the counter and grabbed my coat, sliding it on over my sweater. I didn't leave, though; I just stood there, close enough that you could probably smell the cinnamon on my skin.

— I'll tell you what. You can help me close up. Lock the door, turn off the lights, maybe hold the umbrella over me while I walk to the groomer. If you survive the cat, then we can talk about your vinyl collection. Deal?
